scenes.narration: [serious] One morning, 30,000 computers at an oil giant stopped working.
The company was Saudi Aramco. On August 15, 2012, most workers were at home for a holy night.
That morning, a virus called Shamoon raced through the company. It wiped three out of four office computers.
Where files had been, screens showed a burning American flag.
A group called the Cutting Sword of Justice said they did it. Experts thought that name was fake.
Some U.S. officials blamed Iran, but showed no proof.
Aramco had to buy tens of thousands of new hard drives. One virus emptied an oil giant's offices.

facts.claim: The Shamoon outbreak struck Saudi Aramco on August 15, 2012, hitting about 30,000 workstations; a previously unknown group, the Cutting Sword of Justice, claimed it

The attack began at 11:08 a.m. while more than 55,000 employees were home for Lailat al Qadr; it erased data on about three-quarters of corporate PCs and replaced it with a burning American flag; tens of thousands of hard drives were replaced; researchers saw the group name as a likely red herring
Anonymous U.S. officials blamed Iran-based hackers; U.S. intelligence officials offered no specific evidence
Panetta said more than 30,000 infected computers were rendered useless and had to be replaced, calling it probably the most destructive attack the private sector had seen

seo.title: Shamoon: The Virus That Wiped 30,000 Saudi Aramco Computers
seo.description: In August 2012, the Shamoon virus wiped data on more than 30,000 computers at Saudi Aramco and left a burning flag on screens. U.S. officials blamed Iran, without public proof. Learn what the Shamoon virus did to Saudi Aramco in 2012. #cybersecurity #shamoon #cyberattack #shorts
